paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder whose features overlap with those of Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Affected individuals may have aortic aneurysm and dissection, mitral valve disease, craniofacial findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, and skeletal findings such as tall stature, arachnodactyly and joint hypermobility. Severity varies widely within and between families, and some mutation carriers have no cardiovascular involvement (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015; Kuechler et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported a 9-year-old European-American girl born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents who had 2 older healthy children and no previous miscarriages. From birth she had distal arthrogryposis, with contractures of the fingers and toes, as well as hypotonia, failure to thrive, growth retardation and delayed gross motor development. On examination she had decreased bulk in all appendicular and axial muscles, strength of 1/5, low tone and diminished reflexes throughout. She had markedly reduced subcutaneous fat, a positive Gower sign and a waddling gait. Craniofacial findings included bifid uvula, retrognathia, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, blue sclerae, a metopic ridge, a tubular nose and a midline facial nevus flammeus. Skeletal and connective tissue findings included long narrow hands and feet with arachnodactyly, hyperextensible large joints, mild pectus excavatum, pes planus and coxa valga. Muscle biopsy showed type 1 fiber predominance. She had no cardiac defect or aortic dilatation, no intellectual disability and no scoliosis.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with features overlapping Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome and an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Seven family members, aged 40 to 68 years, had aneurysms and dissections that mainly involved the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta, and 3 died from aortic dissection and rupture. Two had iliac and subclavian artery aneurysms. Four members had mitral valve abnormalities, ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation that required surgery. Craniofacial abnormalities were subtle and included a long face, high-arched palate and retrognathia. Some members had pectus deformity, scoliosis, velvety skin, varices, hiatal hernia, HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease or celiac disease, and 1 had easy bruising. In 2 individuals, aortic tissue showed elastic fiber fragmentation and medial degeneration. A 17-year-old mutation carrier had no documented cardiovascular features but had mild systemic manifestations.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) also described 10 additional families (families 2 through 11) with TGFB3 mutations. Some patients had type A or type B aortic dissection, and 1 died from dissection of a cerebral aneurysm. Some had mitral valve disease, patent foramen ovale, or atrial or ventricular septal defects. Typical Loeys-Dietz syndrome findings were common, including hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, cervical spine instability and clubfoot. Other recurrent features were dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia, tall stature, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity and inguinal hernia. One patient had short stature, and 2 had early-onset osteoarthritis. The medical records showed no evidence of ectopia lentis. Aortic wall tissue showed elastic fiber fragmentation with deposition of collagen and proteoglycans.

paragraphs.text: Across the 11 families, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) summarized 43 patients (23 males and 20 females), not all of whom were evaluated for every feature. Type A dissection occurred in 4 patients (median age 51 years), type B dissection in 6 (median age 44.5 years) and aortic aneurysm in 6. Skeletal findings included tall stature (12), arachnodactyly (16), pectus deformity (8), kyphoscoliosis (11) and joint hypermobility (9). Loeys-Dietz syndrome features included hypertelorism (14), bifid uvula (11) and cleft palate (5). The authors observed striking intra- and interfamilial variability. They found no early arterial dissection, no dissection at small aortic dimensions and no striking arterial tortuosity. Vascular involvement ranged from none at age 64 years to type A or B dissection and death from dissection of a cerebral aneurysm.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) used exome sequencing in a girl with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, hypertelorism, low muscle mass and growth retardation.
